evidence: No reply on this thread. PR7 (a616a17) added a timedOut flag to the async path and a hasTimeout/SIGTERM check to the sync path, confirming the original bug (any signal-terminated exit labeled timeout) was real; the sync half of that fix was itself still imprecise (see cc-candybar#7/F1).
guidance_note: Distinguish 'our timer fired' from 'the child died by signal for any other reason' with an explicit flag set only by the timer callback, not by inferring intent from which signal arrived.

evidence: No reply on this thread. The original diff shows `void launch({detached:true,...})` immediately followed by `return true`, discarding the promise and unconditionally reporting success; PR7 introduced launchDetachedSync returning `result.ok`, confirming the bug was real and fixed later.
guidance_note: Never `void` a promise whose result determines the function's own return value; either await it or make the call synchronous.

evidence: Reviewer itself frames this as unlikely under current workload, so the premise is a real but low-probability gap, not an active bug. PR7 bumped ROLLING_BUFFER_CAP from 4096 to 16384 with a documented rationale, matching one of the two options the reviewer offered.

No reply on this thread. Splitting `command` on whitespace to derive argv is exactly the kind of implicit contract that breaks on quoted args or paths with spaces; PR7 switched execGitAsync to accept args: string[] directly, eliminating the split.
guidance_note: Never reconstruct argv by splitting a command string on whitespace; accept args as an array at the API boundary so the contract can't silently mis-tokenize.

evidence: No reply on this thread. The finding is accurate but low-impact (kill on an already-exited pid is a harmless ESRCH on most platforms). PR7 added a `!settled` guard before `child.kill('SIGTERM')`, confirming the fix.

narrative: PR6 merged only two minutes after it was opened, before Copilot's single review round was even posted, so none of its 8 findings ever got a reply on the original thread. All 8 were nonetheless real (verified against the follow-up PR's diff), and all were fixed within about 20 minutes in PR7 rather than through the address-pr-reviews reply flow. The fix chosen for F6 (making byCategory sparse) was itself under-thought and produced three fresh findings in PR7.
guidance_observations: Merging before the automated reviewer finishes means every finding on that PR starts life with no reply thread, breaking the plan/fix/reply traceability the address-pr-reviews skill is built around.

A fix that changes a data structure's key-population rule (dense-with-zeros to sparse) needs to be checked against every downstream consumer's assumptions (formatter, wire version, iteration order) in the same pass, not iteratively via more review rounds.

evidence: The named fix for cc-candybar#6/F2 correctly added a `timedOut` flag on the async path but, on the sync path, approximated timeout-vs-signal with `hasTimeout && result.signal === 'SIGTERM'` — a child that self-terminates via SIGTERM for an unrelated reason while a timeout option happens to be set is still mislabeled 'timeout'. Verified against current HEAD of src/proc/launch.ts: this exact `hasTimeout`/`SIGTERM` heuristic is still present today, unfixed.
guidance_note: A heuristic proxy (signal type + option presence) is not the same fix as tracking whether the local timer actually fired; the sync path needed its own explicit timedOut-equivalent flag, not a signal/option correlation.

evidence: The comment added by the F6 fix claims byCategory and the histograms have 'same shape', but byCategory is populated in onStart while histograms are populated only in onEnd via recordDuration, so an in-flight-only category appears in one and not the other — the comment overstates a guarantee the code doesn't provide.
guidance_note: Do not write a symmetry claim into a comment unless both sides are populated by the same event; state the actual invariant (populated at start vs. at completion) instead.

evidence: Verified via git show a616a17: before the F6 fix, byCategory was built by iterating the stable LAUNCH_CATEGORIES array; after, it iterates the `subprocessCount` Map, whose key order depends on which category happened to fire first in that daemon process. This is a genuine behavioral regression (stable order to run-dependent order), not a pre-existing gap.
guidance_note: When switching a serialized map's construction from a fixed enum order to iteration over a mutation-order Map, either sort before serializing or keep a stable index alongside the sparse filter.

evidence: Verified via git show a616a17: the formatter's `n > 0` filter was removed on the assumption the snapshot is already sparse, but the protocol version was not bumped, so an old v2 daemon (which still densely fills byCategory with zeros) paired with a new client would print every zero-count category again -- exactly the bug the F6 fix was supposed to eliminate, now reintroduced for the mixed-version window.
guidance_note: Removing a defensive filter because 'the producer now guarantees X' is only safe once every possible producer (including older still-running daemon versions across a protocol boundary) actually guarantees X; a wire-protocol change needs a version bump or the filter needs to stay.

evidence: The F3 fix made spawnDaemonDetachedReal return `result.ok` instead of always `true`, closing the 'silent success' bug, but the caller still only sees a bare boolean and discards `result.reason`/`result.error`, so ENOENT/EACCES/EAGAIN are visible as failure but not diagnosable -- a real but narrower remainder of the same underlying problem (spawn failure detail lost).
guidance_note: When fixing 'failure is reported as success', also check whether the failure detail (reason/error) that made the diagnosis possible is being propagated to the caller, not just the boolean success/fail bit.

evidence: launchDetachedSync is a brand-new exported function created by the F3 fix; the reviewer's concern is about the new function's own type signature (it accepts the full LaunchOpts, including timeoutMs/stdinInput/detached:false, none of which it honors), which is a fresh design gap in the new code rather than a regression of prior behavior.
guidance_note: When promoting an internal helper to an exported API, give it a narrower parameter type that only includes what it actually supports, instead of reusing the broader internal options type.

narrative: PR7 itself merged within 3 minutes of creation, before its own single review round posted, so none of its 6 findings got a reply either. Five of the six (F1, F2, F3, F4, F5) trace directly to two of PR6's fixes: the sync-path timeout heuristic from F2 (still wrong today, verified in current HEAD) and the byCategory sparsification from F6 (which alone produced three separate new findings: a false comment, a lost stable ordering, and a mixed-version wire regression). This is the batch's clearest case of a single fix costing more review debt than it resolved.
guidance_observations: The byCategory sparsification (cc-candybar#6/F6's fix) is a textbook example of a fix that needed a design pass, not a quick patch: it touched ordering, comment accuracy, and wire compatibility simultaneously and got none of the three right on the first attempt.

Because both PR6 and PR7 merged before their own reviews posted, the batch has no example of the agent replying 'Fixed in <sha>' on either PR's threads -- the follow-up PR pattern substitutes for, but does not restore, thread-level traceability.

evidence: Unguarded subscriber callbacks in an async IIFE can reject and surface as an unhandled rejection; the reply routes both initial-delivery call sites through a shared safeInvoke() try/catch, matching the existing refreshSubscribers pattern, with new contract tests pinning the behavior.

Snapshotting the callback Set once at fire-time and calling every snapshotted callback allows delivery to a subscriber that unsubscribed mid-flight; the fix re-checks Set membership at each call site so unsubscribe is a hard delivery guarantee, which is exactly what the cited law describes (the current membership decides, not a stale snapshot).

The reply-hint says 'pushback' but the reply opens 'Good catch' and adds real trailing-edge debounce (refreshing/refreshAgain sets, doRefreshLoop) with a contract test asserting at most two fetches under a 10x invalidation burst -- a full accept-and-fix, not a pushback; the reply-hint is a lexical artifact of the opening clause's tone.

Verified against the code: src/powerline.ts constructs a bare `new GitService()` only as a fallback when deps.gitService is not injected, and it does not import GitDataProvider; the daemon's render cache always injects the provider, so the uncached path is genuinely confined to the demo/tests as the pushback claims. Both proposed alternatives (import GitDataProvider into powerline.ts, or add a second TTL cache) would have created either an upward dependency or a duplicate cache, so declining both and leaving a documented escape hatch is the sound call.
guidance_note: A pre-kz8.3 cache being removed from a lower layer is fine as long as the layer boundary is audited for every call site that could reach production without the new cache injected, not just the obvious ones -- this pushback did that audit explicitly and it held up.

evidence: Flagged [ON-NAMED-FIX-COMMIT 791f324] but this is a false positive: `git show 1f878e9:src/daemon/cache/git.ts` (the original round-0 diff, before 791f324) already has the identical bug -- repoRoot resolved from workingDir via findGitRoot, but the actual fetch uses `this.inner.getGitInfo(workingDir, options, projectDir)`, which can land on projectDir instead. 791f324 (the F1-F3 fix) never touched this code path. The cross-repo contamination is real and the resolveEffectiveGitDir fix in c1942d6 is a correct, well-tested resolution -- it just wasn't caused by the named commit.
guidance_note: When a cache key is derived from one resolution path but the actual fetch can use a different effective path (workingDir vs. projectDir here), key the cache off whichever value the fetch itself will resolve to, computed once and shared by both.

evidence: Flagged [ON-NAMED-FIX-COMMIT 791f324] but false positive: the refresh path's `this.getGitInfo(entry.workingDir, ...)` call (which re-resolves repoRoot via a redundant git rev-parse on every refresh) is identical in the original round-0 diff (1f878e9) and in 791f324 -- the coalescing fix added a wrapper loop around the same call, it didn't introduce the extra shell-out. The fix in c1942d6 (extracting getGitInfoForRoot to skip re-resolution) is real and verified by a call-count contract test.
guidance_note: A per-repo refresh loop that already knows the resolved key should call an internal fetch-by-key helper, not the public entry point that re-derives the key from scratch.

evidence: Flagged [ON-NAMED-FIX-COMMIT c1942d6] but false positive: getGitInfoForRoot's cache-miss path has no in-flight coalescing in either the round-0 original (1f878e9) or in c1942d6 -- c1942d6 only changed how the cache key/effective dir was resolved, not miss handling. The concurrent-miss race under Promise.all-driven parallel rendering is real and the fetchInFlight Map added in a7d6535 is a correct, tested fix.
guidance_note: A cache whose explicit purpose is eliminating duplicate subprocess work needs miss-coalescing (an in-flight promise map) from the first version, since parallel callers racing a cold cache is the normal case for a render pipeline that builds lines with Promise.all.

evidence: Flagged [ON-NAMED-FIX-COMMIT c1942d6] but false positive: the 'microtask after subscribe() returns' comment text is present verbatim in the original round-0 diff (1f878e9) and unchanged by c1942d6. The overstatement is real (delivery follows async gitDir resolution plus a possible git shell-out, not a microtask) and the reworded comment in a7d6535 is accurate.

Flagged [ON-NAMED-FIX-COMMIT c1942d6] but false positive on causation: SourceRegistry's constructor already imported and constructed GitDataProvider in the round-0 original (1f878e9), untouched by c1942d6. The substantive dlog leak was real and correctly fixed by swapping to the neutral logger. But the closing line -- '[LAW:one-way-deps] -- the runtime law is satisfied' -- misapplies the citation: one-way-deps is about the import edge (var-system still imports a file under src/daemon/cache/), not about runtime side effects; removing dlog fixed the side effect but left the actual dependency-direction violation the reviewer named untouched, so citing the law to justify deferring the structural fix overstates what was actually resolved.
guidance_note: A law about dependency direction is not satisfied by removing a dependency's side effects while leaving the import edge itself in place; either move the file or acknowledge the law is still open, don't declare it satisfied.

evidence: Reply-hint says 'pushback' but the reply is a full accept ('Caught'), correctly identifying this as a pre-existing bug the refactor inherited. Flagged [ON-NAMED-FIX-COMMIT a7d6535] but false positive on causation: watcherTargets(repoRoot) is byte-identical between the round-0 original (1f878e9) and a7d6535 -- the worktree-unaware .git/HEAD path assumption predates every fix in this PR. The gitDir-based rewrite in 0467cfd is a real, tested fix.
guidance_note: Any code path that assumes `<repoRoot>/.git` is a directory needs to special-case the worktree case (.git as a gitdir-pointer file) from the first version that touches watcher or mtime paths, since worktrees are a normal, not exotic, git usage pattern.

evidence: Verified via git show: c1942d6's test helper was `function tick(times = 4)`; a7d6535 (the fix commit for F7's concurrent-miss coalescing, per its own commit message 'Replaced the fragile microtask-count tick(N) helper with setImmediate') rewrote it to `function tick(_times = 1)` without implementing the loop, so existing `tick(10)` call sites silently ran only once. This is a genuine regression introduced as a side effect of the F7 fix's accompanying test rewrite, not a pre-existing bug.
guidance_note: Renaming an unused parameter with a leading underscore to silence a lint warning is a signal to double check the parameter was actually meant to be unused; here it was supposed to drive a loop and the rename hid that the loop had been deleted.

evidence: Flagged [ON-NAMED-FIX-COMMIT 0467cfd] but the true cause is one round earlier: the dlog-to-debug swap that silenced watcher error logging was made in a7d6535, the fix commit for F9 (var-system/daemon coupling) -- confirmed by the agent's own reply text ('the pass-3 dlog to debug swap fixed var-system's leak but silenced daemon observability'). The logger-injection fix in eefffa0 (daemon passes dlog, var-system keeps the neutral default) correctly resolves the regression without reintroducing the coupling.
guidance_note: When removing a daemon-specific side effect (a log writer) from shared code to fix a layering leak, inject the logger instead of deleting it outright, so the layer that actually wants the observability doesn't lose it as collateral damage.

evidence: Sibling of F12: the same a7d6535 dlog-to-debug swap silenced GitDataProvider's own invalidate/evict/subscriber-exception logging. Fixed identically via logger injection in eefffa0. The bundled resolveGitDir try/catch addition is correctly framed as a trust-boundary exception to no-defensive-null-guards rather than a silent-skip violation of it -- the fallback returns a value every caller already handles, it never throws past the guard.

Before F10's fix (0467cfd), watcherTargets always received repoRoot, whose refs/heads reliably exists, so the unconditional refs/heads dir target never hit ENOENT. F10's fix switched the parameter to the resolved gitDir, which for worktrees is a metadata dir without refs/heads -- making the pre-existing unconditional target newly ENOENT-prone. The noise only became visible in daemon.log after F12/F13 restored dlog injection, but the code defect itself originates in F10's incomplete worktree handling. The stat-check-before-including fix in 7d61eea is correct and verified against the diff.
guidance_note: When making a path resolution worktree-aware, audit every fixed assumption that depended on the old (always-main-repo) path shape -- here, that refs/heads exists -- not just the specific files the finding named.

evidence: Verified via the diff hunk itself: the exact comment text this finding flags as wrong ('.git/HEAD, .git/index, .git/refs/heads') was written by 7d61eea, F14's own fix commit, replacing an older GitPoller-era comment. The new wording was inaccurate the moment it was written -- it names literal .git/* paths and an unconditional refs/heads, when the provider actually watches the resolved gitDir and conditionally includes refs/heads per F14's own fix.
guidance_note: When a fix changes what a piece of code actually does, and that fix also touches a nearby comment describing the old behavior, the rewritten comment must describe the new behavior precisely (resolved gitDir, conditional refs/heads) rather than restating a simplified version of the old one.

narrative: PR8 is the batch's only PR with real back-and-forth review (it stayed open ~5 hours, giving Copilot 8 passes). Most mid-PR findings carry an ON-NAMED-FIX-COMMIT flag, but checking each one against the actual pre-fix diff shows five of them (F5, F6, F7, F8, F10) are false positives: pre-existing bugs from the original round-0 diff that Copilot simply hadn't surfaced yet, not regressions from the named commit. The genuine fix-caused chains are narrower but real: F7's coalescing fix broke a test helper (F11), F9's dlog-removal fix silenced daemon logging twice (F12, F13), and F10's worktree fix was incomplete (F14) whose own correction then left a stale comment (F15). Every finding was eventually accepted and correctly fixed except F4 (a well-supported full pushback) and F9 (accepted the real bug, but the pushback half leaned on a law citation that overstated what was actually resolved).
guidance_observations: The ON-NAMED-FIX-COMMIT flag marks 'raised against a commit that was named as an earlier fix', not 'caused by that fix' -- five of ten flagged findings in this PR turned out to be pre-existing bugs the reviewer simply had not reached yet, verified by diffing the named commit against the original round-0 diff.

Reply-hint mismatches were common in this PR: F3, F5, F8, F10, and F11 were hinted as 'pushback' or 'unclear' but read as full accept-and-fix on the actual text -- the hint tracks the reply's opening clause tone ('Caught', 'Fair', 'Good catch') rather than the substance.

The three genuine fix-caused chains share a pattern: a fix correctly closes the named finding but changes an adjacent surface (a test helper, a logger, a comment) without auditing what depended on the old state of that surface.

evidence: No reply on this thread (PR merged 6 seconds after creation, before the round-0 review posted). Verified against later history: commit 3d04efc's follow-up 'fix(termcols): fall back to stderr.columns, not stdout.columns' (addressing Copilot review on the duplicate PR #10) explicitly confirms stdout is the captured statusline pipe in the Claude hook flow and stderr is the attached TTY -- exactly this finding's claim -- and the current HEAD of src/index.ts reads process.stderr.columns.
guidance_note: For a CLI invoked as a hook whose stdout is captured (not a TTY), always check stderr for TTY-backed properties like terminal width, never stdout.

evidence: No reply on this thread. Same underlying defect as F1, in the daemon-side resolver; confirmed fixed later (current HEAD of src/utils/terminal-width.ts checks process.stderr.columns, not stdout.columns) via the same follow-up commit referenced for F1.
guidance_note: A pure resolver and its wire-boundary caller should agree on which stream is the TTY-backed fallback; both were wrong here for the same reason and needed the same fix.

evidence: No reply on this thread. Overriding process.stdout.columns via defineProperty and restoring only the value (not the descriptor) leaves a shadowing own-property that can leak across test files -- a real test-isolation bug. A later commit's message ('test: restore property descriptor, not the value, for stderr.columns') confirms this exact class of issue was eventually fixed, addressing Copilot review on the duplicate PR #10.
guidance_note: When monkey-patching a getter-backed property for a test, capture and restore the original property descriptor (or delete the override), not just a remembered value, so the restoration doesn't itself leave a permanent own-property.

evidence: No reply on this thread. Same descriptor-restoration defect as F3, in a different test file; covered by the same later fix referenced for F3.

narrative: PR9 merged 6 seconds after it was created -- before any review could possibly land -- so all 4 findings arrived on already-merged code with no reply thread engaged. All 4 are genuine bugs, two of them functionally serious (the fallback the whole PR exists to provide, terminal width detection, was checking a pipe instead of the TTY, defeating the PR's stated purpose in the common Claude-hook case). None were fixed within this batch's PR9; a duplicate PR (#10, closed, same title) and a later consolidated merge (#13) eventually applied fixes matching every one of these findings almost verbatim, but that work sits outside this batch's scope.
guidance_observations: Three of this batch's four PRs (6, 7, 9) merged in under three minutes, before Copilot's review posted, leaving 18 of 33 findings in this batch with no reply on the original thread despite the substance being valid in nearly every case.

The core defect here (checking stdout instead of stderr for TTY width in a hook context) is exactly the kind of thing a quick manual smoke test against a real Claude Code hook invocation would have caught before merge, since the PR's entire premise (capture width at the wire boundary) was silently defeated by it.
